walkthroughs.body_html:
Introduction to Economics — a core area of Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Introduction to Economics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Introduction to Economics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Ricardo published 'Principles of Political Economy and Taxation' in:
What is the difference between nominal and real values?
options: Nominal means estimated and real means accurate.
A monopoly is when one country dominates world trade.
Nominal values are written and real values are spent.
Nominal values are measured in current money; real values are adjusted for inflation to allow meaningful comparison over time.

mcqs.q: What components make up aggregate demand?
options: Aggregate demand is just the total amount consumers want to buy.
Nominal values are written and real values are spent.
AD = C + I + G + (X - M): consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. A shift in any component shifts the AD curve.
Aggregate demand is the same as GDP measured by demand.

mcqs.q: Are monopolies always bad for consumers?
options: Nominal values are written and real values are spent.
A monopoly is when one country dominates world trade.
Standard theory says monopolies restrict output and raise prices, but possible benefits include economies of scale, R&D investment and dynamic efficiency.
Monopolies are illegal and always harmful.
